<h1 class="graf graf--h1">I Got Lost in <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">client-go</code>. Here's the Map I Wish I Had.</h1>
<p class="graf graf--p"><em class="markup--em markup--p-em">A first-time contributor's guide to understanding what everything does and why it matters.</em></p>
<hr>
<h2 class="graf graf--h2">The First Day is Confusing — That's Normal</h2>
<p class="graf graf--p">The first time I cloned <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">k8s.io/client-go</code>, I opened the directory and counted about 30 top-level folders. <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">dynamic</code>, <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">tools</code>, <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">util</code>, <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">informers</code>, <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">listers</code>, <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">transport</code>... I didn't know where to start.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p">Here's the thing nobody tells you upfront: <strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">most of those folders exist to solve one specific problem</strong>, and once you understand the problem, the solution makes immediate sense. This article is my attempt to hand you that understanding before you need it — not after three hours of <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">grep</code>-ing through source code.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p">We'll go from "how do I even connect to the cluster" all the way to "how does a production controller actually work." Every section points you to the exact files so you can follow along.</p>
<hr>
<h2 class="graf graf--h2">First, What Is <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">client-go</code> Actually?</h2>
<p class="graf graf--p">It's the official Go library for talking to a Kubernetes API server. Not the Kubernetes types themselves (those live in <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">k8s.io/api</code>) — just the <strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">client machinery</strong>: HTTP connections, caches, queues, and the scaffolding for writing controllers and operators.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p">If you've ever used <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">kubectl</code>, that's a program that uses this library under the hood. If you've ever written a Kubernetes operator, you've used this library too.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p">Think of it in three layers stacked on top of each other:</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Your business logic             │
├──────────────────┬──────────────────────┤
│  Typed / Dynamic │  Informers +         │
│  API clients     │  Workqueue           │
├──────────────────┴──────────────────────┤
│         rest / transport                │
│   (TLS, auth, rate limiting, retries)   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
              Kubernetes APIServer
</code></pre>
<p class="graf graf--p">The bottom layer is plumbing you configure once. The middle layer is the API you use to read and write cluster state. The top is where your actual logic lives. Let's go layer by layer.</p>
<hr>
<h2 class="graf graf--h2">Step 1: Getting a Connection</h2>
<h3 class="graf graf--h3"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">rest.Config</code> — Your Cluster Credential Bundle</h3>
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Where it lives:</strong> <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">rest/config.go</code></p>
<p class="graf graf--p">Everything starts with <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">rest.Config</code>. It's a simple struct that holds everything needed to connect to the API server: the URL, TLS certificates, authentication token, and client behavior tuning.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p">There are two common ways to get one, depending on where your program runs:</p>
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Inside a Pod</strong> (the production case):</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">config, err := rest.InClusterConfig()
</code></pre>
<p class="graf graf--p">Kubernetes automatically mounts a service account token and CA cert into every Pod. <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">InClusterConfig()</code> just reads those. No kubeconfig needed.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">On your laptop</strong> (local development):</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">config, err := clientcmd.BuildConfigFromFlags("", "/path/to/kubeconfig")
</code></pre>
<p class="graf graf--p">This reads the same <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">~/.kube/config</code> file that <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">kubectl</code> uses.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p">A few knobs on <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">rest.Config</code> that matter in practice:</p>
<ul class="postList graf graf--ul">
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">QPS</code> and <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">Burst</code></strong>: how fast your client is allowed to hit the API server. Defaults are conservative (5 req/sec, burst 10). Controllers talking to busy clusters often need this tuned up.</li>
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">Timeout</code></strong>: per-request deadline.</li>
</ul>
<blockquote class="graf graf--blockquote graf--pullquote">
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Tip:</strong> Open <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">rest/config.go</code> and read the field comments. It's dense but worth it — those comments are the real documentation.</p>
</blockquote>
<hr>
<h2 class="graf graf--h2">Step 2: Reading and Writing Cluster State</h2>
<p class="graf graf--p">With a <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">rest.Config</code> in hand, you build a client. Here's where you hit your first fork in the road.</p>
<h3 class="graf graf--h3">Option A: Typed Clientset (for built-in resources)</h3>
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Where it lives:</strong> <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">kubernetes/clientset.go</code></p>
<p class="graf graf--p">If you're working with standard Kubernetes resources — Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, and so on — use the typed clientset. It gives you autocomplete, compile-time type checking, and readable method chains:</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">clientset, err := kubernetes.NewForConfig(config)

// List all running pods in "default"
pods, err := clientset.CoreV1().Pods("default").List(ctx, metav1.ListOptions{})

// Scale a deployment
dep, err := clientset.AppsV1().Deployments("default").Get(ctx, "my-app", metav1.GetOptions{})
dep.Spec.Replicas = ptr.To[int32](5)
_, err = clientset.AppsV1().Deployments("default").Update(ctx, dep, metav1.UpdateOptions{})
</code></pre>
<p class="graf graf--p">The pattern is consistent: <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">clientset</code> → <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">ApiGroup()</code> → <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">Resource(namespace)</code> → <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">Action()</code>.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p">One thing that trips people up early: <strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">update conflicts</strong>. Kubernetes uses optimistic concurrency — every object carries a <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">resourceVersion</code>, and if two writers update the same object simultaneously, one of them gets a <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">409 Conflict</code>. The right response is to re-fetch and retry:</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">retry.RetryOnConflict(retry.DefaultRetry, func() error {
    dep, err := deploymentsClient.Get(ctx, "my-app", metav1.GetOptions{})
    if err != nil { return err }
    dep.Spec.Replicas = ptr.To[int32](1)
    _, err = deploymentsClient.Update(ctx, dep, metav1.UpdateOptions{})
    return err
})
</code></pre>
<blockquote class="graf graf--blockquote graf--pullquote">
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Runnable example:</strong> <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">examples/create-update-delete-deployment/</code> — this is a good first thing to run against a real cluster.</p>
</blockquote>
<h3 class="graf graf--h3">Option B: Dynamic Client (for CRDs and unknown resources)</h3>
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Where it lives:</strong> <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">dynamic/interface.go</code></p>
<p class="graf graf--p">The typed clientset only knows about Kubernetes built-in APIs. If you're working with Custom Resources (CRDs), or building a tool that needs to handle arbitrary resource types without being recompiled, you want the dynamic client.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p">The trade-off is real: you lose compile-time type checking. Objects come back as <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">*unstructured.Unstructured</code> — essentially a <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">map[string]interface{}</code> that mirrors the JSON payload. You access fields through helper functions instead of struct fields.</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">client, err := dynamic.NewForConfig(config)

deploymentGVR := schema.GroupVersionResource{
    Group: "apps", Version: "v1", Resource: "deployments",
}

result, err := client.Resource(deploymentGVR).Namespace("default").Get(ctx, "my-app", metav1.GetOptions{})

// Reading fields from an unstructured object
replicas, found, err := unstructured.NestedInt64(result.Object, "spec", "replicas")
</code></pre>
<p class="graf graf--p">My rule of thumb: if you know at compile time what resource type you're dealing with, use the typed clientset. If you don't — because you're building something generic, or working with CRDs that don't have generated clients — use dynamic.</p>
<blockquote class="graf graf--blockquote graf--pullquote">
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Runnable example:</strong> <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">examples/dynamic-create-update-delete-deployment/</code></p>
</blockquote>
<hr>
<h2 class="graf graf--h2">Step 3: The Part That Makes Controllers Actually Work</h2>
<p class="graf graf--p">Raw API calls are fine for one-shot scripts or CLI tools. But controllers and operators need to <strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">watch for changes and react continuously</strong> — and this is where most tutorials get vague right when things get interesting.</p>
<h3 class="graf graf--h3">The Problem With Polling</h3>
<p class="graf graf--p">The naive approach is to list all your objects every few seconds. It works, but it hammers the API server, introduces lag, and doesn't scale. Real controllers use a smarter model: <strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">list once, then watch for changes</strong>.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p">The <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">tools/cache</code> and <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">util/workqueue</code> packages implement this model. Once you understand them, Kubernetes controller code starts to feel inevitable rather than magical.</p>
<hr>
<h3 class="graf graf--h3"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">tools/cache</code> — The Informer Stack</h3>
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Where it lives:</strong> <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">tools/cache/shared_informer.go</code>, <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">tools/cache/delta_fifo.go</code></p>
<p class="graf graf--p">The informer is your local replica of cluster state. It does three things:</p>
<ol>
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Lists</strong> all objects of a type to get a consistent starting snapshot</li>
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Watches</strong> for changes from that point forward, updating its local cache</li>
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Notifies your handlers</strong> when objects are added, changed, or deleted</li>
</ol>
<p class="graf graf--p">Here's how the pieces connect:</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">APIServer
   │  LIST + WATCH
   ▼
Reflector ──► DeltaFIFO ──► Indexer (local cache)
                                   │
                           your event handlers fire
</code></pre>
<ul class="postList graf graf--ul">
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Reflector</strong>: the bit that actually talks to the API server. It handles reconnects and relists transparently.</li>
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">DeltaFIFO</strong>: a queue where each key accumulates its deltas (Added, Updated, Deleted) before being processed.</li>
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Indexer</strong>: the in-memory cache you read from. It supports secondary indexes (by namespace, by label, etc.).</li>
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">SharedIndexInformer</strong>: multiplexes all of this across multiple handlers. Five controllers watching the same resource type share <em class="markup--em markup--p-em">one</em> watch connection.</li>
</ul>
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">The rule that matters most:</strong> your event handlers must be fast. They run on the informer's internal goroutine — if you block them with slow API calls or heavy computation, you back up the entire watch stream. The pattern the docs enforce is:</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">// CORRECT: handler just enqueues a key
AddFunc: func(obj interface{}) {
    key, _ := cache.MetaNamespaceKeyFunc(obj)
    queue.Add(key)   // ← this is ALL the handler should do
},

// WRONG: heavy work in handler
AddFunc: func(obj interface{}) {
    // don't: clientset.CoreV1().Pods("ns").Update(...)  ← blocks the watch path
},
</code></pre>
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Another rule you'll hit if you skip it:</strong> always wait for the cache to sync before starting your workers.</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">factory.Start(ctx.Done())
if !factory.WaitForCacheSync(ctx.Done()) {
    return fmt.Errorf("cache sync timed out")
}
// now it's safe to start workers
</code></pre>
<p class="graf graf--p">If you don't wait, your workers will read from an empty cache and make decisions based on no data. This is one of those bugs that only shows up in production under timing pressure.</p>
<hr>
<h3 class="graf graf--h3"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">informers</code> Package — The Typed Factory</h3>
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Where it lives:</strong> <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">informers/factory.go</code></p>
<p class="graf graf--p">The top-level <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">informers</code> package wraps <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">tools/cache</code> in a nicer API. <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">SharedInformerFactory</code> is a registry that creates typed informers on demand and ensures only one informer exists per resource type.</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">factory := informers.NewSharedInformerFactory(clientset, 30*time.Second)

podInformer := factory.Core().V1().Pods()
depInformer := factory.Apps().V1().Deployments()

podInformer.Informer().AddEventHandler(...)

factory.Start(ctx.Done())
factory.WaitForCacheSync(ctx.Done())
</code></pre>
<p class="graf graf--p">Useful options when creating the factory:</p>
<ul class="postList graf graf--ul">
<li class="graf graf--li"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">WithNamespace("prod")</code> — if your controller only cares about one namespace, scope it.</li>
<li class="graf graf--li"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">WithTweakListOptions(fn)</code> — add a label selector so you only watch objects you care about.</li>
<li class="graf graf--li"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">WithTransform(fn)</code> — strip fields you don't need to reduce memory. (Be careful: this runs on the hot path.)</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h3 class="graf graf--h3"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">util/workqueue</code> — Where Retries Live</h3>
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Where it lives:</strong> <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">util/workqueue/queue.go</code>, <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">util/workqueue/rate_limiting_queue.go</code></p>
<p class="graf graf--p">This package is the bridge between your event handlers and your reconcile workers. It solves problems that aren't obvious until you've hit them:</p>
<ul class="postList graf graf--ul">
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Your handler fires 50 times for the same object</strong> because the Pod kept flapping. You don't want 50 reconcile runs — you want one.</li>
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Your reconcile fails</strong> because a dependent resource isn't ready yet. You want to retry, but not immediately, and not forever.</li>
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Two workers shouldn't reconcile the same object at the same time</strong>, because they'd race each other.</li>
</ul>
<p class="graf graf--p">The workqueue handles all three with its <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">dirty</code> / <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">processing</code> internal model:</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">queue.Add("default/my-pod")
        │
        ▼
   [dirty: default/my-pod]
        │
   queue.Get()
        │
        ▼
   [processing: default/my-pod]   ← worker runs here
        │
   queue.Done("default/my-pod")
        │
        ▼
   [clean — or queued again if Add was called while processing]
</code></pre>
<p class="graf graf--p">The critical guarantee: if you Add the same key 10 times while a worker is busy, it still only processes once after the current run finishes. No duplicates.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">The canonical worker loop</strong> (memorize this shape):</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">func (c *Controller) processNextItem() bool {
    key, quit := c.queue.Get()
    if quit {
        return false
    }
    defer c.queue.Done(key)   // ← always, always defer this

    err := c.reconcile(key)
    if err == nil {
        c.queue.Forget(key)         // success: clear backoff history
        return true
    }

    if c.queue.NumRequeues(key) &lt; 5 {
        c.queue.AddRateLimited(key) // retry with exponential backoff
        return true
    }

    c.queue.Forget(key)             // give up; drop the item
    runtime.HandleError(err)
    return true
}
</code></pre>
<p class="graf graf--p">Two things people mix up:</p>
<ul class="postList graf graf--ul">
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">Done(key)</code></strong> — releases the queue's lock on that key. The queue needs this to let the key be processed again.</li>
<li class="graf graf--li"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">Forget(key)</code></strong> — clears the rate limiter's memory of how many times this key has failed. Without this on success, future retries for the same key will carry an inflated backoff.</li>
</ul>
<p class="graf graf--p">They're completely independent. <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">Forget</code> does not call <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">Done</code>. <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">Done</code> does not call <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">Forget</code>. Both are necessary, in the right places.</p>
<blockquote class="graf graf--blockquote graf--pullquote">
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Runnable example:</strong> <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">examples/workqueue/</code> — run this. Read every line. It's the clearest illustration of the full pattern.</p>
</blockquote>
<hr>
<h2 class="graf graf--h2">Putting It Together: The Full Controller</h2>
<p class="graf graf--p">Everything above clicks together in a structure that looks like this (from <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">docs/quickstarts/controller-skeleton.md</code>):</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">type Controller struct {
    client kubernetes.Interface
    lister corev1listers.PodLister   // reads from local cache
    synced cache.InformerSynced
    queue  workqueue.TypedRateLimitingInterface[string]
}

func (c *Controller) reconcile(ctx context.Context, key string) error {
    ns, name, _ := cache.SplitMetaNamespaceKey(key)

    pod, err := c.lister.Pods(ns).Get(name)  // ← reads from cache, not API
    if apierrors.IsNotFound(err) {
        return nil   // already gone, nothing to do
    }
    if err != nil { return err }

    // do your logic here
    // write back via c.client (Patch or SSA preferred over Update)
    _ = pod
    return nil
}
</code></pre>
<p class="graf graf--p">Notice the reconcile function reads from the <strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Lister</strong> (the local cache), not directly from the API server. The object in the cache is often <strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">newer</strong> than the event that triggered the reconcile — and that's fine, even desirable. You always want to act on the latest known state.</p>
<hr>
<h2 class="graf graf--h2">High Availability: Leader Election</h2>
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Where it lives:</strong> <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">tools/leaderelection/</code>, <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">examples/leader-election/</code></p>
<p class="graf graf--p">When you run multiple replicas of your controller for redundancy, you need exactly one of them actively writing to the cluster. <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">tools/leaderelection</code> handles this by competing for a <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">Lease</code> object in the API:</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">leaderelection.RunOrDie(ctx, leaderelection.LeaderElectionConfig{
    Lock:            leaseLock,
    LeaseDuration:   15 * time.Second,
    RenewDeadline:   10 * time.Second,
    RetryPeriod:     2 * time.Second,
    ReleaseOnCancel: true,
    Callbacks: leaderelection.LeaderCallbacks{
        OnStartedLeading: func(ctx context.Context) {
            controller.Run(ctx, 2)
        },
        OnStoppedLeading: func() {
            os.Exit(0)
        },
    },
})
</code></pre>
<p class="graf graf--p">One sharp edge worth knowing: leader election is <strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">coordination, not fencing</strong>. If you set <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">ReleaseOnCancel: true</code> but your goroutines keep making API writes after the context is cancelled, another replica can win leadership while your stale work continues in parallel. Make sure guarded work actually stops before you release the lease.</p>
<blockquote class="graf graf--blockquote graf--pullquote">
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Runnable example:</strong> <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">examples/leader-election/</code> — run two instances with different <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">-id</code> flags and watch failover happen live.</p>
</blockquote>
<hr>
<h2 class="graf graf--h2">Testing Without a Real Cluster</h2>
<p class="graf graf--p"><strong class="markup--strong markup--p-strong">Where it lives:</strong> <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">testing/</code>, <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">examples/fake-client/</code></p>
<p class="graf graf--p">For unit tests, there's <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">fake.NewSimpleClientset()</code> — an in-process fake that records which API calls your code made:</p>
<pre class="graf graf--pre"><code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">fakeClient := fake.NewSimpleClientset(existingPod)
// pass fakeClient to your controller
// then assert on fakeClient.Actions() afterward
</code></pre>
<p class="graf graf--p">Fake clients are great for verifying that your controller made the right API calls with the right arguments. They're not great for testing behavior that depends on real server semantics — things like field defaulting, Server-Side Apply ownership, or real watch timing.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p">For those cases, reach for an integration test framework like <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">envtest</code> (from <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">controller-runtime</code>) or just spin up a <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">kind</code> cluster.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p">There's also a subtle timing issue when using fake clients with informers: writes between the initial LIST and the watch connection being established can be silently missed. The <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">examples/fake-client/main_test.go</code> shows how to handle this correctly — worth a read.</p>
<hr>
<h2 class="graf graf--h2">The Cheat Sheet</h2>
<div class="table-image-container">
                        <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Table table-1" class="graf graf--image" />
                    </div>

<h2 class="graf graf--h2">One Last Thing</h2>
<p class="graf graf--p">Contributing to <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">client-go</code> directly isn't quite how it works — this repository is a staging mirror. The actual source lives at <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">kubernetes/kubernetes</code> under <code class="markup--code markup--pre-code">staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/</code>. Changes made there are automatically synced here every day.</p>
<p class="graf graf--p">So if you want to contribute: submit your PR to the main Kubernetes repo. This repo is where downstream projects consume the library from.</p>
<hr>
<p class="graf graf--p">Good luck in there. It's a big codebase, but once the informer + workqueue pattern clicks, almost everything else makes sense.</p>
